title: Baptism
summary: The cited New Testament passages connect baptism with making disciples, repentance, belonging to a community, and sharing in Christ’s death and life. They describe these connections in different settings; baptism should not be collapsed with the Lord’s Supper, which is the subject of 1 Corinthians 11.
historical_context: Matthew 28 places baptism in Jesus’ commission to make disciples, Acts 2 narrates people receiving the message and being baptized, and Romans 6 uses baptism to explain life in relation to Christ’s death and resurrection. These passages show how the New Testament texts present baptism; this object has no separate historical source on earlier Jewish washings or later church practice.
canonical_context: In Matthew 28:18–20, Jesus commands his followers to make disciples, baptizing and teaching them. Acts 2:37–41 connects baptism with repentance, forgiveness, the gift of the Holy Spirit, and being added to the community. Romans 6:1–11 uses baptism into Christ as part of Paul’s argument that those who share his death are to live in newness of life. First Corinthians 11:23–26, by contrast, discusses the Lord’s Supper. It is a related communal practice, but it is not a baptism passage.
literary_context: The references use different forms: Matthew 28 is a commissioning scene, Acts 2 narrates the response to Peter’s speech, Romans 6 develops an argument about sin and new life, and 1 Corinthians 11 gives instruction about the communal meal. Read the baptism passages within their immediate arguments, and keep Paul’s discussion of the meal distinct from his discussion of baptism.
covenantal_significance: Matthew 28 links baptism with becoming disciples; Acts 2 places it within a response that includes repentance, forgiveness, and the Spirit; and Romans 6 connects baptism with participation in Christ’s death and a new way of life. Together these passages associate baptism with belonging and formation, while making different points about its place in discipleship and Christian life.
canonical_role: Baptism serves as an institutional anchor, connecting social practice, worship, leadership, and covenant life across related passages and themes.

interpretive_notes.note: Baptism and the Lord’s Supper are distinct practices in the cited texts. Matthew 28, Acts 2, and Romans 6 discuss baptism; 1 Corinthians 11:23–26 concerns the communal meal. The latter may provide broader worship context, but it does not directly support a claim about baptism.

Romans 6 explains baptism within Paul’s argument about sharing Christ’s death and living a changed life; it does not describe the ritual’s mode or settle every question about baptism’s effect. Matthew 28 and Acts 2 emphasize discipleship and communal response in their own settings.
